progression.startsWith: Remember the bottle that gave no change in all three tests? It could be cyclohexane, or it could be 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol that leaves dichromate orange. But one of them has an O H group and the other doesn't. An infrared spectrum shows bonds directly, so it can settle this quickly.
progression.stopsAfter: reading the axes, assigning O–H (alcohol and acid), C–H, C=O, N–H and C–O, using shape, combination and missing bands, and stating what IR cannot show.
progression.nextLesson: NMR (route chem-m8-c11, delivered as c11a then c11b).

teaching.task: One bottle gave no change in all three tests, so it could be cyclohexane or a tertiary alcohol. How can shining infrared light through the sample show which bonds are there?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the tests stalled; IR shows bonds directly (1); (2) bonds vibrate; a bond absorbs the infrared that matches its vibration, so a dip appears (2); (3) transmittance, dips down, wavenumber backwards (3); (4) stiffer bonds and lighter atoms vibrate faster, so higher wavenumber; where the spring analogy breaks (4); (5) the data sheet gives the ranges; four rows do most of the work (5); (6) C–H is nearly everywhere, so it rarely decides (6); (7) alcohol O–H: hydrogen bonds weaken each O–H by different amounts, so the band is broad (7); (8) acid O–H: paired molecules, two hydrogen bonds, lower and very broad, plus a C=O (8); (9) C=O strong and sharp; shows a carbonyl, not which kind (9); (10) N–H narrower and weaker (10); (11) fingerprint region: match, don't assign; a strong C–O still useful (11); (12) the routine and a missing band as evidence (12); (13) bottle Y solved (13); memory aid (14); attempts (15 to 18); decision rule and handoff (19); key notes (20).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Remember the bottle that gave no change in all three tests? It could be cyclohexane, or it could be 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol that leaves dichromate orange. Every covalent bond vibrates, a bit like two balls joined by a spring. Up the side is transmittance, the percentage of light that gets through. Think of the spring again. You don't need to memorise where each bond absorbs, because the data sheet gives the ranges. Start with C H. Now the O H in an alcohol. A carboxylic acid has an O H too. The C equals O dip is one of the easiest to spot: strong and sharp, between sixteen eighty and seventeen fifty. Primary and secondary amines have N H bonds, which absorb from thirty-three hundred to thirty-five hundred, overlapping the alcohol O H range. Below about fifteen hundred, the spectrum gets crowded. So here's a routine. Back to the bottle. Here's a picture to remember: beard plus sword means acid. Your turn. Both candidates have a C equals O, so the dip at seventeen forty doesn't decide. Last one. Green only shows something was oxidised, and aldehydes do that as well as primary and secondary alcohols. So, when you meet an infrared spectrum, scan from left to right.
teaching.openingDecision: Remember the bottle that gave no change in all three tests? It could be cyclohexane, or it could be 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol that leaves dichromate orange. But one of them has an O H group and the other doesn't. An infrared spectrum shows bonds directly, so it can settle this quickly.
teaching.understandingCheck: Your turn. Compound X is either butanoic acid or ethyl ethanoate. Use the spectrum and the band values on the card to identify X, and justify your answer. Pause here to answer. Last one. Liquid Z is either an alcohol or an aldehyde, and it turns acidified dichromate green. Use the spectrum on the card to identify the type of compound, and explain why the dichromate result alone couldn't. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope:
Syllabus dotpoint (as printed; NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p58; C8-IQ2-02 is this project's local catalogue ID, not a code printed in the syllabus), quoted from ../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y12.json:

"investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
- proton and carbon-13 NMR
- mass spectrometry
- infrared spectroscopy (ACSCH130)"

design.visualSystem: spectra are coded only (new IR trace part; never an AI image of a spectrum); every spectrum is realistic for its named compound and each band is listed under "Numbers to verify" for checking against NIST or SDBS; the instrument is one existing painted plate; the vibrating bond is a coded abstract diagram (balls and spring, no people); no people, hands or faces; at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; one reasoning stage at a time; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question and its spectrum or band list kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (answer, key reason, one crossed mistake, about 15 to 30 s); original HSC-style questions only; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims ("points to", "supports", "fits", "rules out" only for a missing band against a stated candidate list).

(violet), "2 O–H (acid): 2500 to 3000, very broad?" (violet), "3 C=O: 1680 to 1750, strong?" (red), "4 C–O: 1000 to 1300, strong?" (amber). the bottle Y plate and its three chips return small at left. the board clears. the board clears. the card stays, shrunk to the top. question card, worded as printed (A2 under Decisions). the card stays, shrunk to the top. the board clears. Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".
